frase_gancho.texto: Little animals beneath a rain cloud and over flowering squash plants.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue along your route: the small reliefs of the slope tell the same story, but at the scale of an animal.

guion_corto.texto: A few steps from El Rey there are small reliefs that look little like him. They are Monuments Six, Seven and Eight, carved on rocks exposed by the rain. One shows a little animal crouching beneath a rain cloud. Others show animals over flowering squash plants. Eulalia Guzmán documented them in nineteen thirty-four. All of them are near a stream that carries rainwater down the slope. Grove explains that they share a theme with El Rey: the relationship between caves and rain, fertility and cosmic power. Notice that the scenes are small: you have to look for them patiently. Both speak of the same thing, water and fertility.

guion_largo.texto:
After the great relief, the small ones. Just a few meters from El Rey there are small reliefs that Eulalia Guzmán documented in nineteen thirty-four. They present a theme that repeats.

One shows a little animal crouching beneath a rain cloud. Others show animals over flowering squash plants. Grove numbers them as Monuments Six, Seven and Eight.

All of these reliefs are near a stream that carries rainwater down the slope. The whole setting is very close to water. That closeness is no accident: the theme of the scenes is rain and what rain makes grow.

Squashes are a clear example. A flowering squash plant is the moment when the plant prepares to bear fruit. Grove offers no interpretation of the species of animal, so we speak only of little animals.

Crouching means curled up, with the body close to the ground. It is the posture that Grove describes in the little animal beneath the rain cloud.

Squash was an important crop in Mesoamerica. That it appears in flower, next to animals and rain, brings three things together: the water of the sky, the growing plant and the beings that surround it.

Compare these reliefs with those at the base of the hill. There, great boulders show supernatural animals dominating people. Here, on a small scale, animals appear beneath the rain or among the plants. The two groups are different, but they share the rock as their support.

Arqueología Mexicana recalls that, in that region, settlements were located near springs, water holes and rivers. At Chalcatzingo, water was not only used: it was also drawn in stone.

The rain that left the site exposed, in nineteen thirty-four, is the same rain that stars in these reliefs. It is a coincidence worth noticing.

If you cannot find all three reliefs, do not be discouraged. The sources consulted do not specify which ones can be seen today, and some are small. Look for the rain cloud, the crouching little animal and the flowering squash plant: those are the images Grove describes.

El Rey and these animals share raindrops and squashes. For Grove, they have in common a theme that must have been obvious, both to Guzmán and to the peoples of the Middle Preclassic. It is the link between caves and rain, fertility and cosmic power.

That link explains why these scenes were engraved next to a stream. Grove writes that even today it remains a strong image.

If you go back to [El Rey](chz_17_monumento_1_el_rey) after seeing these reliefs, the scene changes scale. What seemed merely majestic becomes part of a single story about water.

A practical warning: these reliefs are small and are on rocks, so you may have to search for them patiently.
